newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico president lashes out at foreign press.
newsitem.headline: Mexico president lashes out at foreign press.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo has lashed out at the foreign press, telling his ambassadors that correspondents painted a distorted picture of Mexico as a one-party dictatorship, newspapers reported on Wednesday.

"Frequently they want to stereotype us; they want to present us as if we were sometimes ridiculous, like the last dictatorship, like the last totalitarian regime of those inherited from the start of this century," Zedillo told Mexican ambassadors on Tuesday.

Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) has ruled Mexico uninterrupted for the past 67 years, winning every election with often dubious tactics. This has led some critics to dub the country "the perfect dictatorship," in the words of Peruvian novelist Mario Vargas Llosa.

Until recently, the PRI held a virtually absolute monopoly on the presidency, congress and all state governorships, town halls and state assemblies. It also controlled the labour movement, youth and women's groups and almost all public posts.

In the past few years, however, the opposition has made big inroads into the PRI's control. Conservatives and left-wingers now hold scores of town halls, several governorships and a sizeable proportion of state deputies.

Zedillo has repeatedly said he wants to open up Mexico's political system further but he complained to the ambassadors that a biased foreign press was not giving his government the credit it deserved. He was especially critical of "some Mexicans" who, he said, made a living out of "publicizing, reproducing, generating and feeding a mistaken image of the country."

"In order to do this, (these Mexicans) meet with (foreign) correspondents to receive them in their homes at the weekend until they convince them that Mexico will go on being ... the perfect dictatorship," he charged.

Zedillo, a publicity-shy technocrat whose early career was at Mexico's central bank, has had an uneasy relationship with the media since taking office. He initially broke with tradition by announcing plans for monthly news conferences -- previously taboo here -- but quickly dropped the idea after reporters asked what aides said were "inappropriate questions."
